$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-258 TRANCHE 7 — the migration package, the
generated client location, and the expand/contract rollout rehearsal. One
entry per guard, each carrying the file it lives in, the EXACT text that
implements it (`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), and the NAMED cases
that were seen to go red (`kills`).
PATHS ARE REPOSITORY-RELATIVE, not package-relative as in the six ledgers
beside it. This tranche's guards straddle two packages: the rehearsal's own
machinery lives in `internal-packages/tenancy-database`, because that is the
ONE Prisma home and the only place entitled to rebuild an old release's
client, while the store half lives here. The ledger is filed here because
this is where the mutation ledgers are hashed and counted, and a seventh
file in a directory that already has six is easier to find than a first file
in a directory that has none.
WHAT THIS TRANCHE'S GUARDS ARE, AND WHY THEY NEEDED WORK TO BE FALSIFIABLE.
Most of them validate INPUTS that are correct in this repository — the
migration set is well-ordered, the frozen schemas hash to their pins — so
their refusal branches were unreachable as first written. `orderedMigrations`
now takes an injectable root and the two digest checks are pure functions,
so every refusal has a case that builds the broken input it exists for.
One branch stayed unreachable and is DECLARED rather than counted.
procedure: PROVE THE SUITES GREEN FIRST, and with a non-zero executed-case count. A
run that fails to load is indistinguishable from a kill, and tranche 1's
first sweep reported twenty-two kills that were all of that kind.
For one entry: replace its `from` with its `to` in the named file — the
driver requires the `from` to occur EXACTLY ONCE, so a stale entry is an
error and not a silent no-op — run the named suites against a real
PostgreSQL container on the Mac mini, and confirm a NAMED case in `kills`
is among the failures. Then revert and confirm green again.
TWELVE OF THE SIXTEEN NEED NO DATABASE, and that is a property of this
tranche rather than a weakness: the migration-set and frozen-schema guards
are decisions about FILES, and a container would add nothing to them. The
four that do need one are M-T7-11 through M-T7-16's database entries, where
the thing being measured is what PostgreSQL did to a legacy database.
THE DRIVER IS AD HOC, as in the six tranches before this one. Each entry
below was applied, run and reverted individually.

mutations.name: M-T7-01 the bootstrap records the repository's genesis checksum, not the legacy one
mutations.note: The migration runner is HAPPY either way, which is why this needed an assertion of its own rather than a reliance on `migrate deploy` refusing. Without the patch the database claims a genesis no installation ever had.
kills: the ordered migration set is total and gap-free, and the database applied exactly it

mutations.name: M-T7-02 the migration set may hold two directories on one stamp
kills: the ordered migration set > refuses a set whose stamps collide, because the filesystem then decides
mutations.note: THE SWEEP CHANGED THE CODE for this one: it SURVIVED the first pass, because a set with two directories on one stamp also fails the order comparison two lines later and the two guards answered the same code. Five distinct codes were minted so each case can tell its guard from the one behind it.

mutations.name: M-T7-03 a directory that is not a stamp and a label is admitted
mutations.note: A nullish off-by-one rather than a deletion: `exec` answers null, never undefined, so the branch is skipped and the stamp read from it is read off null.
kills: the ordered migration set > refuses a directory that is not a stamp and a snake_case label

mutations.name: M-T7-04 a stray file beside the migration directories is ignored
kills: the ordered migration set > refuses a stray file beside the migration directories

mutations.name: M-T7-05 the set need not begin at the genesis migration
kills: the ordered migration set > refuses a set that does not begin at the genesis migration

mutations.name: M-T7-06 the frozen baseline SQL is applied whatever it now says
kills: the frozen release schemas > refuses a frozen baseline SQL that no longer hashes to its pin

mutations.name: M-T7-07 a frozen release schema is rebuilt whatever it now says
kills: the frozen release schemas > refuses a schema that no longer hashes to its pin

mutations.name: M-T7-08 a schema with no generator output line is generated unchanged
mutations.note: The guard that stops a rebuild writing over the LIVE client. Both frozen schemas name the live output path, so a silent no-match would generate an old release's datamodel into the directory the rest of the package imports.
kills: the frozen release schemas > refuses a schema with no generator output line to redirect

mutations.name: M-T7-09 the renamed column is taken from a difference of any size
kills: addressing a renamed column without spelling it > refuses when the two datamodels differ by more than one stored field
addressing a renamed column without spelling it > refuses when they differ by none, because then there is nothing to rehearse

mutations.name: M-T7-10 a relation field counts as a stored column
mutations.note: A relation is not a column, so counting one would make the whole-table column sweep compare a name PostgreSQL has never heard of.
kills: addressing a renamed column without spelling it > counts scalar and enum fields and nothing else

mutations.name: M-T7-11 a delegate the rebuilt client does not expose is handed back anyway
kills: addressing a renamed column without spelling it > refuses a delegate the rebuilt client does not expose

mutations.name: M-T7-12 the catalogue difference never reports a column that went
mutations.note: The renamed column is the ONLY thing this half of the difference reports, and it is the sharpest contract-phase operation in the set.
kills: the measured catalogue difference holds no operation outside the declared set

mutations.name: M-T7-13 a mandatory column with a DEFAULT counts as narrowing
mutations.note: The whole expand/contract distinction for an added column. NOT NULL WITH a default is invisible to a writer that never names it; without one it is a refusal.
kills: the measured catalogue difference holds no operation outside the declared set

mutations.name: M-T7-14 the legacy attachment is left unbound to a turn
mutations.note: Proves the fixture is what satisfies the m4 ownership preflight, and therefore that the rehearsal is running the REAL backfill rather than a migration that found nothing to do. THE SWEEP CHANGED THE SUITE for this one: the refusal originally reached `beforeAll`, which executed zero cases and read as VACUOUS rather than as a kill, so the upgrade's own refusal is now captured into a variable a named case asserts.
kills: the ordered migration set is total and gap-free, and the database applied exactly it

mutations.name: M-T7-15 the store rehearsal starts from an empty database, not a legacy one
mutations.note: The single edit that would turn the store half back into the clean-install rehearsal every other harness in the directory already runs.
kills: the V1 stores read the tenancy tree a legacy release wrote

mutations.name: M-T7-16 the rollout partner is the legacy release rather than the binary being replaced
mutations.note: Two old binaries are open in this tranche and confusing them would make the backward direction claim the wrong thing.
kills: the binary being replaced reads back what the V1 stores wrote

declared-unfalsifiable.name: D-T7-01 the lexicographic and numeric orders of the migration stamps agree
declared-unfalsifiable.guard: for (let index = 1; index < stamps.length; index += 1) { ... if (!(Number(current) > Number(previous))) throw ... }
why: UNREACHABLE BY CONSTRUCTION, and left in place anyway. The migration name
rule admits only names whose stamp is EXACTLY fourteen digits, and
equal-length digit strings order the same way lexicographically and
numerically. So no set the name rule accepts can reach this branch, and no
mutation of it can be killed. Removing it would be the tidier answer and is
the wrong one: the branch is the tripwire for the day the width rule is
relaxed, which is the only way the two orders could ever part.
It is recorded HERE rather than counted as a kill because a ledger that
counted it would be claiming a sweep result it did not have. The PROPERTY
is checked by a named case — `orders by name and by number identically,
which is why the order is total` — which asserts the agreement and the
fixed width on the set that actually ships.

result: SIXTEEN ENTRIES, SIXTEEN KILLS, NONE VACUOUS, plus ONE DECLARED
UNFALSIFIABLE. Each kill is a NAMED case in its entry's `kills` list, seen
red on the Mac mini at branch head against real PostgreSQL where the entry
needed one. All three suites were proved green and non-empty before anything
was mutated: 17 executed cases in the guard suite, 9 in the binary-level
rehearsal and 6 in the store-level one.
WHAT THE SWEEP CHANGED ABOUT THE WORK, rather than only confirming it. Six
of these guards could not be killed as first written, because their inputs
were the repository's own correct files and no case could hand them a broken
one. `orderedMigrations` grew an injectable root and the two digest checks
became pure functions for that reason alone. A guard nobody can turn red is
not evidence, and finding six of them in one tranche is worth saying plainly.
M-T7-01 IS THE ONE TO LOOK AT. The bootstrap patches the genesis row's
checksum to the LEGACY release's, and `prisma migrate deploy` is perfectly
happy without that patch — it compares the recorded checksum against this
repository's own file, which is what an unpatched row already holds. So the
guard was invisible to every case until one asserted the row carries the
frozen baseline's digest AND that the two digests differ. Without it the
rehearsal would have been running against a database in a state no
installation has ever been in, and reporting a clean result.
